finding.claim: The /fetch handler passes the attacker-supplied `target` query parameter straight to http.Get and streams the full response body back to the caller. There is no host, scheme, or IP validation, so any unauthenticated client can make the server request arbitrary internal or external URLs and read the results (full-read SSRF).
finding.sink: main.go:16 — http.Get(target); response echoed via io.Copy(w, resp.Body) at main.go:22

trace.note: Route /fetch is registered to the unauthenticated fetch handler
Server listens on :8080 (all interfaces), no auth middleware
Attacker-controlled `target` read from the query string, no validation
http.Get(target) dispatches the request; default client follows up to 10 redirects, so redirects to 169.254.169.254 or RFC-1918 hosts are also followed
Upstream response body is copied verbatim to the HTTP response, so the attacker reads the internal response

finding.guards_checked: None on the path from main.go:15 to main.go:16. No allowlist, no url.Parse, no scheme check (Go's http client only accepts http/https, so file:// is not exploitable), no auth middleware, no redirect restriction (no CheckRedirect set). Severity HIGH: no allowlist and no auth barrier, and the response is returned to the caller. Deployment exposure is not visible from the code, so network reachability is assumed.

verdict.guard_found: none on the /fetch path. The allowlist `allowed` (main.go:9-12) and the hostname check (main.go:27) exist only in safeFetch, which is registered on /safe (main.go:42). fetch at main.go:14-23 uses the raw `target` with no url.Parse, host check, or CheckRedirect. The redirect-following at main.go:16 is the default client behavior, as the candidate says.
verdict.reason: The /fetch route (main.go:41) hands the unauthenticated query value `target` (main.go:15) to http.Get (main.go:16) and copies the response body back to the client (main.go:22) with no validation, while the allowlist guard at main.go:27 protects only the separate /safe handler. Deployment exposure is not visible in the code; the listener on :8080 (main.go:43) is assumed reachable.

finding.claim: NOT A FINDING. The /safe handler (safeFetch) is closed by a strict allowlist: url.Parse, then exact map membership on u.Hostname(), before http.Get. Userinfo and port tricks (e.g. http://images.example.org@169.254.169.254/) fail because Hostname() returns the real host. Residual risk only: http.Get follows redirects from allowlisted hosts without re-checking the target. Exploiting that needs an allowlisted host to misbehave (for example an open redirect), which falls under trusted-service failure, so it is not reported.

trace.note: Short-circuit: err check first, then exact map lookup on u.Hostname() — strict set membership, fail-closed on case or trailing-dot variants

finding.guards_checked: Strict hostname membership (map lookup, not substring/regex) enforced before the network call; parse error handled before dereferencing u; fail-closed on non-matching host.

verdict.guard_found: main.go:27 `if err != nil || !allowed[u.Hostname()]` is an exact map-membership check on the parsed hostname, returning 403 before the sink. The err check short-circuits, so u is not dereferenced when nil.
verdict.reason: The source (main.go:26, r.URL.Query().Get("target")) is attacker-controlled, but the exact hostname allowlist at main.go:27 is a closing guard that runs before http.Get at main.go:31, and the candidate's trace lines all match the code. The redirect-following residual it mentions depends on an allowlisted host misbehaving, so it is not a finding in this code.
